summary: MarsPath AI is an interactive web application designed to plan safer and more efficient exploration routes on Mars. While the shortest path is often assumed to be the best, the Martian terrain presents hidden risks such as steep slopes and rough surfaces. To address this challenge, our solution leverages a 20-meter native resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the Jezero Crater alongside NASA Mars Trek cartography. By calculating a movement cost that factors in distance, local slope, and topographic roughness, our A* search algorithm allows users to compare fast, safe, and balanced routes. Operating entirely on the frontend without the need for a backend server, MarsPath AI provides operators with vital data—including elevation profiles, accumulated ascent/descent, and calculated risk—transforming raw topographic data into clear, actionable navigation decisions.
details:
Executive Summary MarsPath AI is an interactive web application designed to plan and optimize exploration routes on Mars. It serves as a decision-support tool for robotic missions by evaluating topographic risks and calculating the most efficient and safe paths using real Martian elevation data.

1. Project Description

1.1. What does it do? MarsPath AI calculates and compares alternative navigation routes (fast, safe, and balanced) between a starting point and a destination on the Martian surface. It identifies topographic risks—such as steep slopes and rough terrain—that are not visible on standard 2D cartographic maps.

1.2. How does it work? The application loads a 20-meter native resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the Jezero Crater alongside NASA Mars Trek cartography (WMTS). It uses an A* search algorithm running directly in the browser. The algorithm evaluates a grid of cells, calculating a movement cost based on a custom formula: cost = distance × (1 + slope_weight × slope + roughness_weight × roughness). The user can set a maximum slope and select the mission objective to get an automated route recommendation.

1.3. Innovation and purpose The core innovation is its "frontend-only" architecture. By packaging the DEM as a static resource and running the A* pathfinding engine entirely in the user's browser, the application eliminates the need for a backend, Python, or a database. Its purpose is to transform static topographic data into an interactive, real-time decision-making tool.

1.4. Benefits and impact

  • A. Social, environmental, and technological benefits: Technologically, it provides a highly scalable, backend-free solution that runs on any modern browser. Socially, it makes complex planetary navigation accessible and understandable to the general public.
  • B. Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) or space missions: It directly supports space exploration initiatives (aligning with SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) by providing a framework to safeguard multi-million-dollar rover equipment from hazardous terrain.
  • C. Expected impact on the community: It serves as a powerful educational tool for students and space enthusiasts, helping them understand the real-world constraints of planetary navigation.

1.5. Objectives and expected results The primary objective is to provide a reliable tool to minimize rover traversal risks. Expected results include delivering accurate path comparisons, elevation profiles, and calculated movement costs in a user-friendly interface.

1.6. Methodology and work plan

  • Project phases and schedule:
      1. Data Acquisition & Processing.
      2. UI/UX Design & Base Map Integration.
      3. Algorithm Development (A* engine).
      4. Testing & Deployment.
  • Main activities per stage: Downloading the Jezero DEM, connecting NASA WMTS services, deriving slope/roughness variables, implementing the pathfinding logic, and deploying the Vite project.
  • Intermediate deliverables: DEM static asset extraction, basic map render with coordinates, routing algorithm prototype, and final interactive UI.
  • Example: Data downloads (M20_JezeroCrater_CTXDEM_20m.tif), algorithm logic diagrams, and progress screenshots of the map layers.

1.7. Methodology and tools

    • 1.7.1. Tools and software used: NASA Mars Trek (WMTS), Git, GitHub.
    • 1.7.2. Programming language and framework: React, TypeScript, Vite, CSS.
    • 1.7.3. Hardware and sensors: No specific external hardware or sensors were required; the project is a software-based web application optimized for standard computer browsers.

1.8. Project Management

Team Chart:

Sixto Jhair Sanchez Estela (Team Owner): Lead of Application Deployment and Troubleshooting. Responsible for managing the production environment (deployment) and handling system errors, ensuring the stable execution of the A* routing engine and map integration on the frontend.

Brayan Alexander Villanueva Quispe: UI/UX Designer and Frontend Developer. Responsible for designing the visual interface and writing the core frontend code, focusing on the interactive map components and the planning panel.

Jose Jaime Rodrigo Castro: UI/UX Designer and Frontend Developer. Collaborated on crafting the user experience, structuring the layout, and coding the frontend application to ensure a smooth interaction with the NASA data layers.

Aldomaro Herrera Saucedo: Quality Assurance (QA) and Tester. Tasked with conducting rigorous system tests, evaluating the route generation logic, and providing critical feedback to refine the user experience and improve application stability.

1.9. Location and project location Cajamarca, Peru.

Project Justification

1.10. Impact and Benefits

  • Relevance to NASA mission / alignment with strategic objectives: NASA's Mars missions require extreme caution when moving rovers like Perseverance. By utilizing NASA/JPL data (HiRISE, CTX, MOLA, and the 20m DEM), MarsPath AI aligns perfectly with NASA's objective of ensuring mission safety and longevity by mitigating physical risks during surface operations.

1.11. Expected Results The application successfully maps optimal routes in seconds, providing operators with vital telemetry estimates before movement: total distance, accumulated ascent/descent, maximum/average slope, and a visual risk profile.

1.12. Conclusions and future improvements

  • Lessons learned: Handling and processing large DEM grids strictly on the client side requires careful memory management and efficient heuristic optimization in the A* algorithm to prevent browser freezing.
  • Possible optimizations: Future versions will incorporate rover-specific mobility constraints, estimated energy consumption, dynamic obstacles (like deep sand or individual rocks), communication windows with orbiters, and historical mission data overlays.
